2018 Fund Returns

Multiple linear regression · Nine predictors · Diagnostics and inference

Load the two datasets

Read the ETFs.csv and MutualFunds.csv files in data/. it does not download or load price files. Blank entries are treated as missing values (NA).

etfs <- read.csv("data/ETFs.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
mutualfunds <- read.csv("data/MutualFunds.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))

Keep the relevant columns

Keep a fund identifier, the eight source variables needed for the predictors, and only the 2018 calendar-year fund return. Category returns are benchmark returns, so they are not our response. Trailing and quarterly returns are also excluded. Returns remain in their original decimal units: 0.05 means 5%.

response <- "fund_return_2018"

columns <- c(
  "fund_symbol", "fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio",
  "total_net_assets", "inception_date", "asset_stocks", "asset_bonds",
  "annual_holdings_turnover", "fund_price_earning_ratio",
  "fund_sector_technology", response
)

etfs <- etfs[, columns]
mutualfunds <- mutualfunds[, columns]

# Identify fund type before combining the datasets.
etfs$etf_indicator <- 1
mutualfunds$etf_indicator <- 0
funds <- rbind(etfs, mutualfunds)

Prepare the nine predictors

Use the annual-report net expense ratio because it is available in both files. Convert ratios and weights from proportions to percentages (0.01 becomes 1%). Use natural logs for assets and P/E; zero or negative values cannot be logged and are marked missing. Age is measured in fractional years to January 1, 2018. Funds launched after that date have no applicable age at the start of 2018.

funds$inception_date <- as.Date(funds$inception_date)
funds$fund_age_years <- as.numeric(
  as.Date("2018-01-01") - funds$inception_date
) / 365.25
funds$fund_age_years[funds$fund_age_years < 0] <- NA

# Replace nonpositive inputs with NA before taking logs.
assets <- funds$total_net_assets
assets[assets <= 0] <- NA
pe <- funds$fund_price_earning_ratio
pe[pe <= 0] <- NA

funds$log_total_net_assets <- log(assets)
funds$log_pe_ratio <- log(pe)
funds$net_expense_ratio_pct <- 100 * funds$fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio
funds$stock_weight_pct <- 100 * funds$asset_stocks
funds$bond_weight_pct <- 100 * funds$asset_bonds
funds$annual_turnover_pct <- 100 * funds$annual_holdings_turnover
funds$technology_weight_pct <- 100 * funds$fund_sector_technology

predictors <- c(
  "etf_indicator", "net_expense_ratio_pct", "log_total_net_assets",
  "fund_age_years", "stock_weight_pct", "bond_weight_pct",
  "annual_turnover_pct", "log_pe_ratio", "technology_weight_pct"
)

# Retain only the identifier, prepared predictors, and the 2018 response.
funds <- funds[, c("fund_symbol", predictors, response)]

Stock and bond weights are included without cash and other holdings, avoiding an automatic sum-to-100% constraint. Missing holdings are left missing, not replaced with zero. Technology weight retains the source's sector-weight meaning; it is not recalculated as a share of total fund assets.

Check missing values and prepare the 2018 sample

funds retains every row and only the 2018 response. model_data_2018 keeps only funds with all nine predictors and a 2018 return.

# Missing predictor counts, shown separately for each fund type.
rbind(
  ETF = colSums(is.na(funds[funds$etf_indicator == 1, predictors])),
  Mutual_fund = colSums(is.na(funds[funds$etf_indicator == 0, predictors]))
)

##             etf_indicator net_expense_ratio_pct log_total_net_assets fund_age_years
## ETF                     0                    15                   30            900
## Mutual_fund             0                   210                   34           3288
##             stock_weight_pct bond_weight_pct annual_turnover_pct log_pe_ratio technology_weight_pct
## ETF                     1036            1036                 950          814                   694
## Mutual_fund             2440            2440                1808         6811                  5516

complete_2018 <- complete.cases(funds[, c(predictors, "fund_return_2018")])
model_data_2018 <- funds[complete_2018, ]

# Compare available rows before and after complete-case selection.
rbind(
  All_funds = table(factor(funds$etf_indicator, levels = c(0, 1))),
  Complete_2018 = table(factor(model_data_2018$etf_indicator, levels = c(0, 1)))
)

##                   0    1
## All_funds     23783 2310
## Complete_2018 13201  564

# Initial check of the relationship between fund type and expense ratio.
cor(model_data_2018$etf_indicator, model_data_2018$net_expense_ratio_pct)

## [1] -0.2336357

In the count table, 0 means mutual fund and 1 means ETF. Complete-case selection can change the mix of funds; missingness is not assumed to be random.

Scope and additional predictors

The source files contain 2021 reporting dates. The predictor measurements are not established as January 2018 observations, so this is an exploratory association model, not a historical forecasting or causal model. Obtain pre-2018 characteristics before making such claims.

Fund category is the strongest candidate to investigate next: it can separate investment strategies (for example, domestic equity, international equity, and bond funds). fund_category exists in these files, but it is not added automatically because categories can be sparse and overlap strongly with stock/bond weights. Check ETF and mutual-fund representation within categories before a category-adjusted comparison. Other useful candidates are verified pre-2018 geographic exposure and market capitalization/style. The available trailing beta fields must not be treated as pre-2018 measures without checking their estimation dates. Avoid adding later returns as explanatory variables.

Different share classes may represent the same underlying portfolio, and funds also share market exposures. Row independence cannot be established from these plots. Fund-family/portfolio identifiers would help assess clustering; HC3 standard errors below do not correct dependence between rows. The surviving funds in this later snapshot may also be unrepresentative of all funds in 2018.

Descriptive tables and box plots

For easier interpretation, the model uses return in percentage points: -0.05 becomes -5. Predictor percentages already use the same convention.

Fit the prespecified multiple linear regression

Each slope describes the association with 2018 return while holding the other predictors fixed. The ETF coefficient is the adjusted ETF-minus-mutual-fund difference in percentage points. Log-variable slopes correspond to a one-unit increase in the natural log, not a one-dollar change in assets.

model <- lm(return_2018_pct ~ etf_indicator + net_expense_ratio_pct +
              log_total_net_assets + fund_age_years + stock_weight_pct +
              bond_weight_pct + annual_turnover_pct + log_pe_ratio +
              technology_weight_pct, data = model_data_2018)
summary(model)

ANOVA and hypothesis tests

The overall F test tests that all nine slopes are zero. The partial F tests below test each term after adjusting for all other predictors. For a single slope, the partial F statistic equals the squared ordinary t statistic. The final comparison explicitly tests H0: the adjusted ETF coefficient is zero. All these classical tests assume independent, constant-variance errors and an adequate mean model; small p-values alone do not establish model adequacy.

null_model <- lm(return_2018_pct ~ 1, data = model_data_2018)
knitr::kable(anova(null_model, model), digits = 5, caption = "Overall F test")

Residual and normal Q-Q plots

Look for a horizontal residual smooth near zero, roughly constant vertical spread, and Q-Q points near the line. The scale-location plot highlights unequal variance. Tail departures and influential observations need attention; normality concerns the model errors, not the predictors or raw returns.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model, which = c(1, 2, 3, 5), id.n = 3)


par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fitted(model), model_data_2018$return_2018_pct,
     pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.2),
     xlab = "Fitted return (%)", ylab = "Observed return (%)",
     main = "Observed versus fitted")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
boxplot(residuals(model) ~ fund_type, col = c("lightblue", "peachpuff"),
        main = "Residuals by fund type", ylab = "Residual (percentage points)")
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2)


par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

par(mfrow = c(3, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (v in predictors[-1]) {
  x <- model_data_2018[[v]]
  plot(x, residuals(model), pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.15),
       xlab = v, ylab = "Residual", cex.lab = 0.8)
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
  lines(lowess(x, residuals(model)), col = "red", lwd = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Collinearity

The correlation plot shows pairwise relationships. VIF checks each predictor against all other predictors together. Values above 5 merit investigation; this is a guide, not an automatic deletion rule.

correlations <- cor(model_data_2018[, predictors])
par(mar = c(12, 12, 3, 2))
image(seq_along(predictors), seq_along(predictors), correlations,
      zlim = c(-1, 1), col = colorRampPalette(c("navy", "white", "firebrick"))(100),
      axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Predictor correlations (blue -1; red +1)")
axis(1, at = seq_along(predictors), labels = predictors, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7)
axis(2, at = seq_along(predictors), labels = predictors, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.7)
for (i in seq_along(predictors)) for (j in seq_along(predictors)) {
  text(i, j, round(correlations[i, j], 2), cex = 0.65,
       col = ifelse(abs(correlations[i, j]) > 0.6, "white", "black"))
}


par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
vif <- sapply(predictors, function(v) {
  auxiliary <- lm(reformulate(setdiff(predictors, v), response = v),
                  data = model_data_2018)
  1 / (1 - summary(auxiliary)$r.squared)
})

Unequal variance and robust inference

The studentized Breusch–Pagan (Koenker) test regresses squared residuals on the predictors; H0 is constant conditional variance. With this large sample, interpret its p-value together with the plots. HC3 standard errors allow unequal variance but still assume independent observations and a suitable mean model. Their large-sample z tests and confidence intervals are a sensitivity check, not a cure for dependence, missing confounders or incorrect timing.

squared_residuals <- residuals(model)^2
variance_model <- lm(reformulate(predictors, response = "squared_residuals"),
                     data = model_data_2018)
bp_stat <- nobs(model) * summary(variance_model)$r.squared
knitr::kable(data.frame(Test = "Studentized Breusch-Pagan", Statistic = bp_stat,
                        df = length(predictors),
                        p_value = pchisq(bp_stat, length(predictors), lower.tail = FALSE)))
Test Statistic df p_value
Studentized Breusch-Pagan 698.071 9 0 
# HC3 covariance: inflate each squared residual by its leverage adjustment.
X <- model.matrix(model)
bread <- solve(crossprod(X))
hc3_weights <- (residuals(model) / (1 - hatvalues(model)))^2
hc3_cov <- bread %*% crossprod(X, X * hc3_weights) %*% bread
hc3_se <- sqrt(diag(hc3_cov))
robust_table <- data.frame(Estimate = coef(model), HC3_SE = hc3_se,
                           z = coef(model) / hc3_se,
                           p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(coef(model) / hc3_se)),
                           CI_lower = coef(model) - qnorm(0.975) * hc3_se,
                           CI_upper = coef(model) + qnorm(0.975) * hc3_se)
knitr::kable(robust_table, digits = 5)

Influential observations

Cook's distance combines residual size and leverage. The 4/n and 2p/n lines are screening guides, not reasons to delete observations. Identify and check funds before deciding whether their records are incorrect or represent a population outside the research question.

cooks <- cooks.distance(model)
leverage <- hatvalues(model)
n <- nobs(model)
p <- length(coef(model))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(cooks, type = "h", main = "Cook's distance", ylab = "Cook's D", xlab = "Row")
abline(h = 4 / n, col = "red", lty = 2)
plot(leverage, rstandard(model), pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.2),
     main = "Leverage and standardized residuals", xlab = "Leverage", ylab = "Standardized residual")
abline(v = 2 * p / n, h = c(-3, 3), col = "red", lty = 2)


par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
influence_table <- data.frame(Fund = model_data_2018$fund_symbol,
                              ETF = model_data_2018$etf_indicator,
                              Cooks_D = cooks, Leverage = leverage,
                              Standardized_residual = rstandard(model))

Box–Cox table and profile plot

Ordinary Box–Cox requires a positive response. Use gross return = 1 + decimal return, the ending value of one unit invested. This has an economic meaning and is positive when loss is less than 100%; no arbitrary minimum-based shift is used. Lambda = 1 is equivalent to the original untransformed regression up to scale and intercept; lambda = 0 models log gross return. The grid-based 95% profile interval is approximate. Transformation does not fix predictor timing, clustering, or omitted variables, and is explored rather than automatically adopted. The selected transformed model has different coefficient units.

model_data_2018$gross_return <- 1 + model_data_2018$fund_return_2018
stopifnot(all(model_data_2018$gross_return > 0))
gross_model <- update(model, gross_return ~ .)
bc <- MASS::boxcox(gross_model, lambda = seq(-5, 5, by = 0.1),
                   plotit = FALSE)
best_lambda <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
cutoff <- max(bc$y) - qchisq(0.95, df = 1) / 2
boxcox_table <- data.frame(Lambda = bc$x, Profile_log_likelihood = bc$y,
                           Inside_95pct_profile_interval = bc$y >= cutoff)
write.csv(boxcox_table, "outputs/boxcox_full_table.csv", row.names = FALSE)
# Display conventional transformations and the optimum; export the full grid.
show_rows <- abs(bc$x - best_lambda) < 1e-8 |
             sapply(bc$x, function(x) any(abs(x - c(-2, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2)) < 1e-8))
knitr::kable(boxcox_table[show_rows, ], digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
Lambda Profile_log_likelihood Inside_95pct_profile_interval

if (any(profile_interval %in% range(bc$x))) {
  cat("The profile interval touches the grid boundary; expand the grid before interpreting it.")
}
plot(bc$x, bc$y, type = "l", xlab = expression(lambda),
     ylab = "Profile log likelihood", main = "Box-Cox profile: gross return")
abline(h = cutoff, lty = 2, col = "red")
abline(v = c(best_lambda, 1), col = c("blue", "darkgreen"), lty = c(1, 2))
legend("bottomright", c("Best grid lambda", "Untransformed (lambda = 1)", "95% cutoff"),
       col = c("blue", "darkgreen", "red"), lty = c(1, 2, 2), cex = 0.8)


model_data_2018$transformed_return <- if (abs(best_lambda) < 1e-8) {
  log(model_data_2018$gross_return)
} else {
  (model_data_2018$gross_return^best_lambda - 1) / best_lambda
}
transformed_model <- update(model, transformed_return ~ .)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(transformed_model, which = c(1, 2, 3, 5), id.n = 3)


par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Do not compare R-squared across the two response scales as evidence of improved prediction. Inspect whether the transformed diagnostic patterns improve; the lambda was selected on this same sample.

Save tables and interpret the findings

write.csv(coefficient_table, "outputs/ols_coefficients.csv")
write.csv(robust_table, "outputs/hc3_coefficients.csv")
write.csv(fit_table, "outputs/model_fit.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(descriptive, "outputs/descriptive_statistics.csv")
write.csv(drop1(model, test = "F"), "outputs/partial_F_tests.csv")
write.csv(influence_table, "outputs/influence_diagnostics.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(Predictor = predictors, VIF = vif), "outputs/vif.csv", row.names = FALSE)

The complete-case sample contains 13765 funds, including 564 ETFs. The adjusted R-squared is 0.289. The adjusted ETF difference is 0.414 percentage points, with HC3 95% interval [-0.236, 1.064]. These are associations in this selected sample, conditional on the measured predictors.

A successful analysis reports where assumptions fail; it does not require all diagnostics to pass. Review residual curvature, variance, tail behavior, influence and VIF before proposing revisions. If prediction becomes the goal, add held-out evaluation, ideally splitting by underlying fund rather than share class. No out-of-sample accuracy is claimed here.

Interpretation of this run

The residual plots show unequal spread and pronounced tail departures from normality. The variance test rejects constant variance. Emphasize the HC3 interval for the ETF comparison: it includes zero, so this model does not provide clear evidence of an adjusted ETF advantage at the 5% level. Stock and bond VIFs are about 6.8; the ETF VIF is about 1.1. Thus the main collinearity concern is asset allocation, rather than the ETF indicator.

The Box–Cox optimum is approximately 2.5 on gross returns. This is an exploratory transformation, not a standard log-return recommendation. Check the transformed Q-Q and variance plots before adopting it. Both models remain limited by predictor timing, possible shared portfolios, and selection into the complete-case sample. Investigate influential funds and consider category controls and nonlinear relationships as next steps; do not remove observations or add terms solely to obtain smaller p-values.

Method references: R's ANOVA documentation and MASS Box–Cox documentation.
